\]
This is a geometric series with first term \(1\) and ratio \(\frac{2}{3}\), so
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n=\frac{1}{1-\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{3}}=3.

Step 0: First, restate the condition in an equivalent “coloring” form and identify the key consequence we will use later.

We are asked for the greatest positive integer \(k\) such that the set of positive integers \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\) can be partitioned into \(k\) subsets
\[
A_1,A_2,\dots,A_k,
\]
with the property:

> For every integer \(n\ge 15\) and for every index \(i\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\), there exist two **distinct** elements \(x,y\in A_i\) such that
\[
x+y=n.
\]

Interpretation: think of each \(A_i\) as a “color class” in a \(k\)-coloring of the positive integers (each integer has exactly one color, i.e., belongs to exactly one \(A_i\)). The condition then says: **within each color class \(A_i\)**, every sufficiently large integer \(n\ge 15\) can be formed as a sum of two distinct elements of that same class.

This implies a necessary “coverage” constraint for each fixed \(i\): for every \(n\ge 15\), the set of all pairwise sums of distinct elements of \(A_i\),
\[
\{x+y:\ x,y\in A_i,\ x\ne y\},
\]
must contain **every** integer in \(\{15,16,17,\dots\}\).

In particular, for a specific \(i\), the condition must hold for the 11 consecutive values
\[
n=15,16,\dots,25,
\]
so \(A_i\) must be large enough and structured enough to realize all these sums with distinct pairs. The maximal possible \(k\) will be limited by how many such “pair-sum coverage” structures can coexist in a partition of \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\).
Step 1: **Derive a concrete “small numbers obstruction” using disjointness and a pigeonhole bound.**

From the condition (given in the problem statement), fix a part \(A_i\). For every \(n\ge 15\), there must exist **distinct** \(x,y\in A_i\) with
\[
x+y=n.
\]
In particular, take the **11 consecutive** values
\[
n=15,16,\dots,25.
\]
For each such \(n\), choose one pair \((x_n,y_n)\) of distinct elements in \(A_i\) such that
\[
x_n+y_n=n.
\]

Now consider how small one of the summands can be. Suppose for some fixed \(n\in\{15,16,\dots,25\}\) we had both summands \(\ge 8\). Then
\[
x_n\ge 8,\quad y_n\ge 8 \implies x_n+y_n\ge 8+8=16.
\]
So for \(n=15\), it is impossible that both summands are \(\ge 8\). Therefore, for \(n=15\), at least one of the two distinct elements must satisfy
\[
\min\{x_{15},y_{15}\}\le 7.
\]
Similarly, for \(n=16\), it is possible that both summands are \(\ge 8\), but for smaller \(n\) in our range we can force small summands as follows:

- For \(n=15\): at least one summand \(\le 7\).
- For \(n=16\): at least one summand \(\le 8\) is always true because if both were \(\ge 9\), then \(x_{16}+y_{16}\ge 9+9=18>16\).
- In general, for each \(n\in\{15,16,\dots,25\}\), if both summands were \(\ge n-8+1 = n-7\), then
  \[
  x_n+y_n \ge (n-7)+(n-7)=2n-14.
  \]
  For \(n\ge 15\),
  \[
  2n-14 \ge 2\cdot 15-14=16.
  \]
  This shows that as \(n\) runs over the consecutive block \(15\) to \(25\), we repeatedly “force” the appearance of small numbers in \(A_i\) (summands from a limited initial segment).

Now we sharpen this to a counting/pigeonhole restriction.

Define the set of “small candidates”
\[
S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}.
\]
Claim: For each \(n\in\{15,16,\dots,25\}\), at least one of the chosen summands \(x_n,y_n\) must lie in \(S\).

Proof of the claim: Fix \(n\in\{15,\dots,25\}\). Assume for contradiction that **both** summands are outside \(S\), i.e.
\[
x_n\notin S \ \text{and}\ y_n\notin S \implies x_n\ge 9,\ y_n\ge 9.
\]
Then
\[
x_n+y_n \ge 9+9=18.
\]
So this cannot cover \(n=15\) or \(n=16\) (since \(15,16<18\)). Thus for \(n=15,16\) the claim holds.

For \(n\ge 17\): if both summands were \(\ge 10\), then
\[
x_n+y_n \ge 10+10=20,
\]
which would fail for \(n=17,18,19\). If both summands were \(\ge 11\), then
\[
x_n+y_n \ge 11+11=22,
\]
which would fail for \(n=17,18,19,20,21\). Continuing this logic across our block up to \(25\), we conclude that in order to hit every value \(n=15,16,\dots,25\) with distinct pair sums, we cannot keep both summands permanently in \(\{9,10,11,\dots\}\) without skipping some of the 11 targets. Concretely, for \(n\le 25\), if both summands were \(\ge 13\), then \(x_n+y_n\ge 26>25\), so at least one summand must be \(\le 12\), and in fact the consecutive coverage forces repeated reuse of the smallest available values, all of which must lie in the bounded interval \(S\).

Hence, across the 11 values \(n=15,16,\dots,25\), the pairs \((x_n,y_n)\) must use elements of \(S\) as at least one summand each time. Since \(S\) has only \(8\) elements, by the pigeonhole principle, there exist at least
\[
\left\lceil \frac{11}{8}\right\rceil = 2
\]
distinct targets \(n\) whose representation uses the **same** small element \(t\in S\) as a summand. That is, for some \(t\in S\), there are at least two distinct integers \(n_1,n_2\in\{15,\dots,25\}\) with
\[
t + u_1 = n_1,\qquad t + u_2 = n_2
\]
for some \(u_1\ne u_2\) in \(A_i\).

This creates the key “forcing obstruction”: once \(k\) becomes large, the disjointness of the partition \(A_1,\dots,A_k\) prevents so many color classes from each containing enough small forced summands to realize all 11 consecutive sums \(15\) through \(25\). Therefore an upper bound on \(k\) can be obtained by counting how many disjoint subsets can sustain this forced small-number summand structure.  

(We will make that upper bound explicit in the next step.)

Step 0: **Set up the parity model for the king’s position and express the goal event.**

1. **Define the state parity variables.**  
   Let the king’s position after \(n\) turns be \((X_n,Y_n)\). Consider parities modulo \(2\):  
   \[
   x\pmod 2\in\{0,1\},\quad y\pmod 2\in\{0,1\}.
   \]
   The target event after \(2008\) turns is:
   \[
   E=\{X_{2008}\ \text{is even and}\ Y_{2008}\ \text{is even}\}.
   \]
   “Both coordinates even” means:
   \[
   X_{2008}\equiv 0 \pmod 2,\qquad Y_{2008}\equiv 0 \pmod 2.
   \]

2. **Use the given starting position.**  
   The problem states the king starts at \((0,0)\). Therefore:
   \[
   X_0=0,\quad Y_0=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad X_0\equiv 0\pmod 2,\ Y_0\equiv 0\pmod 2.
   \]

3. **Classify each possible move by its effect on parity.**  
   On each turn:
   - With probability \(0.1\) it moves to each **edge** neighbor: \((x\pm 1,y)\) or \((x,y\pm 1)\).
   - With probability \(0.05\) it moves to each **diagonal** neighbor: \((x\pm 1,y\pm 1)\).
   - With probability \(0.4\) it stays: \((x,y)\).

   Now track parity changes modulo \(2\):
   - **Edge move:** adding or subtracting \(1\) flips parity of exactly one coordinate.  
     Example: \((x+1,y)\) gives \(X\mapsto X+1\), so \(X\pmod 2\) flips, while \(Y\pmod 2\) stays the same.
   - **Diagonal move:** adding or subtracting \(1\) flips parity of both coordinates simultaneously.  
     Example: \((x+1,y+1)\) gives both \(X\mapsto X+1\) and \(Y\mapsto Y+1\), so both parities flip.
   - **No move:** parities stay unchanged.

4. **Reduce to a Markov chain on the parity state.**  
   Define the parity state at time \(n\) as
   \[
   S_n=(X_n\bmod 2,\ Y_n\bmod 2)\in\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}.
   \]
   From (3), each turn either:
   - flips exactly one of the two bits (edge move), total probability:
     \[
     \underbrace{4\times 0.1}_{\text{four edge neighbors}}=0.4,
     \]
   - flips both bits (diagonal move), total probability:
     \[
     \underbrace{4\times 0.05}_{\text{four diagonal neighbors}}=0.2,
     \]
   - flips neither (stay), total probability \(0.4\).

   Thus, conditional on the current parity state, the parity evolution depends only on these flip patterns and not on the actual integer coordinates.

5. **State the goal in terms of the parity state.**  
   The event \(E\) is exactly:
   \[
   E=\{S_{2008}=(0,0)\}.
   \]

**Conclusion of Step 0:** We have reduced the problem to computing the probability that the parity-state Markov chain satisfies \(S_{2008}=(0,0)\), starting from \(S_0=(0,0)\), where each step flips exactly one parity bit with probability \(0.4\), flips both with probability \(0.2\), and flips none with probability \(0.4\).
Step 1: **Compute the parity transition probabilities for the 4-state Markov chain and set up the recursion to track \(S_n\).**

1. **Recall the reduced parity process from Step 0.**  
   From Step 0, the parity state is
   \[
   S_n=(X_n\bmod 2,\ Y_n\bmod 2)\in\{0,1\}^2,
   \]
   with starting state \(S_0=(0,0)\). Also from Step 0, in each turn:
   - the king flips exactly one coordinate’s parity (edge move) with total probability \(0.4\),
   - flips both coordinates’ parities (diagonal move) with total probability \(0.2\),
   - flips neither with total probability \(0.4\).

2. **Break “flips exactly one coordinate” into two types.**  
   “Flips exactly one coordinate” means either:
   - \(X\)-parity flips but \(Y\)-parity stays (i.e., \((a,b)\mapsto(1-a,b)\)), or
   - \(Y\)-parity flips but \(X\)-parity stays (i.e., \((a,b)\mapsto(a,1-b)\)).

   From Step 0’s counts: there are 4 edge neighbors total, and each edge neighbor has probability \(0.1\).  
   - Two of the edge neighbors change \(x\) by \(\pm1\): \((x\pm1,y)\), giving \(X\)-parity flip.
   - Two change \(y\) by \(\pm1\): \((x,y\pm1)\), giving \(Y\)-parity flip.

   Therefore,
   \[
   \mathbb P(\text{flip }X\text{ only})=2\cdot 0.1=0.2,\qquad
   \mathbb P(\text{flip }Y\text{ only})=2\cdot 0.1=0.2.
   \]
   Check against Step 0 total:
   \[
   0.2+0.2=0.4,
   \]
   consistent with the “exactly one flip” total probability.

3. **Break “flips both coordinates” into its (single) transition type.**  
   From Step 0, diagonal moves change both coordinates by \(\pm1\), so they flip both parities simultaneously.  
   There are 4 diagonal neighbors each with probability \(0.05\), so
   \[
   \mathbb P(\text{flip both})=4\cdot 0.05=0.2,
   \]
   also consistent with Step 0.

4. **Write the complete transition rule on parity states.**  
   For any current parity state \((a,b)\in\{0,1\}^2\), the next state is one of:
   \[
   (a,b)\quad\text{with probability }0.4,
   \]
   \[
   (1-a,b)\quad\text{with probability }0.2,
   \]
   \[
   (a,1-b)\quad\text{with probability }0.2,
   \]
   \[
   (1-a,1-b)\quad\text{with probability }0.2.
   \]
   (Here we used: “no move” probability \(0.4\); “flip \(X\) only” \(0.2\); “flip \(Y\) only” \(0.2\); “flip both” \(0.2\).)

5. **Set up variables for the probability of each parity state at time \(n\).**  
   Define
   \[
   p_n^{(a,b)}=\mathbb P(S_n=(a,b)).
   \]
   Since the chain has 4 states, the update at one step is
   \[
   p_{n+1}^{(a,b)}
   =0.4\,p_n^{(a,b)}
   +0.2\,p_n^{(1-a,b)}
   +0.2\,p_n^{(a,1-b)}
   +0.2\,p_n^{(1-a,1-b)}.
   \]
   This equation comes directly from item (4): to be at \((a,b)\) at time \(n+1\), we must have come from each of the four states that can transition into \((a,b)\), with the corresponding probabilities given above.

6. **Record the initial condition using \(S_0=(0,0)\).**  
   From Step 0,
   \[
   p_0^{(0,0)}=1,\qquad
   p_0^{(1,0)}=0,\qquad
   p_0^{(0,1)}=0,\qquad
   p_0^{(1,1)}=0.
   \]
   (Because the king starts at \((0,0)\), so both parities are even, and all other parity states have probability \(0\) initially.)

**Conclusion of Step 1:** We have explicit one-step transition probabilities on the 4 parity states and a full recursion
\[
p_{n+1}^{(a,b)}
=0.4\,p_n^{(a,b)}
+0.2\,p_n^{(1-a,b)}
+0.2\,p_n^{(a,1-b)}
+0.2\,p_n^{(1-a,1-b)}
\]
with initial values concentrated at \((0,0)\). This recursion will be used in the next step to compute \(p_{2008}^{(0,0)}=\mathbb P(X_{2008}\text{ even},\,Y_{2008}\text{ even})\).
Step 2: **Diagonalize the 4-state parity Markov chain using symmetric/antisymmetric combinations and derive a closed form for \(p_{n}^{(0,0)}\).**

2. **Introduce four linear combinations (eigenmodes).**

Substituting this into the same identity for \(f(2n+1)\),

f(2n+1)=f(2n)+\frac{f(2n)}{3f(n)}
=3f(n)t_n+t_n
=t_n(3f(n)+1).
\]
Thus for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) there exists an integer \(t_n\ge 0\) with
\[
\boxed{\,f(2n)=3f(n)\,t_n,\qquad f(2n+1)=t_n(3f(n)+1)\,}.
\]
We will use this together with condition (3), \(f(2n)<6f(n)\), in the next step to bound \(t_n\) and hence restrict which values \(f(k)\) can take.

Now use that \(f(n)\in\mathbb N\), hence \(f(n)\ge 1\), so we can divide both sides by \(f(n)\) (positive):
\[

Divide both sides by \(3\):
\[

\]
Since \(t_n\) is a nonnegative integer, the only possibilities are
\[

Therefore \(t_n\neq 0\), hence
\[
t_n=1\quad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb N.

So we obtain the tight identities

This means for any \(n\), \(f(n)\) can be built by repeatedly applying the rules depending on whether each step uses an even or odd index. Concretely, every binary step from \(n\) to \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) multiplies the current value by \(3\), and adds \(0\) or \(1\) depending on the parity.

### 1) Closed form via binary expansion
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) have binary expansion
\[
n=(b_m b_{m-1}\cdots b_1 b_0)_2,\quad b_i\in\{0,1\},\quad b_m=1.
\]
Repeatedly apply the recurrences by halving:
- If the last binary digit is \(0\), then \(n=2t\) and \(f(n)=f(2t)=3f(t)\).
- If the last binary digit is \(1\), then \(n=2t+1\) and \(f(n)=f(2t+1)=3f(t)+1\).

Thus, starting from \(f(1)=1\) and moving from the most significant bit down to the least, every time we append a binary digit \(0\) we multiply the current value by \(3\), and every time we append a binary digit \(1\) we multiply by \(3\) and then add \(1\).

Concretely, one obtains the standard expansion
\[
\boxed{\,f(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{m} b_i\,3^i\, } \quad\text{for } n=(b_m\cdots b_0)_2.
\]
We verify this quickly on computed values:
- \(1=(1)_2\Rightarrow f(1)=1\).
- \(2=(10)_2\Rightarrow \sum b_i3^i=1\cdot 3+0=3=f(2)\).
- \(3=(11)_2\Rightarrow 1\cdot 3+1=4=f(3)\).
- \(4=(100)_2\Rightarrow 1\cdot 9=9=f(4)\).
- \(5=(101)_2\Rightarrow 1\cdot 9+1=10=f(5)\).
So the formula matches the base computations from Step 3.

### 2) Reduce the equation \(f(k)+f(l)=293\) to a base-3 digit problem
Using the closed form, \(f(n)\) equals the number whose ternary digits (base \(3\)) are exactly the binary digits of \(n\), i.e. \(f(n)\) is a sum of distinct powers of \(3\) with coefficients \(0\) or \(1\).

First express \(293\) in base \(3\). Compute powers:
\[
3^5=243,\quad 3^4=81,\quad 3^3=27,\quad 3^2=9,\quad 3^1=3,\quad 3^0=1.
\]
Now divide:
\[
293-243=50,
\]
\[
50=0\cdot 81 + 50,\quad 50=1\cdot 27+23,
\]
\[
23=1\cdot 9+14,\quad 14=1\cdot 3+11,
\]
\[
11=3\cdot 3+2\quad\text{(but we must stay within digits }0,1,2\text{)}.
\]
Let’s do it cleanly by coefficients \(a_5a_4a_3a_2a_1a_0\) with \(a_i\in\{0,1,2\}\):
- \(a_5=\left\lfloor 293/243\right\rfloor=1\), remainder \(293-243=50\).
- \(a_4=\left\lfloor 50/81\right\rfloor=0\), remainder \(50\).
- \(a_3=\left\lfloor 50/27\right\rfloor=1\), remainder \(50-27=23\).
- \(a_2=\left\lfloor 23/9\right\rfloor=2\), remainder \(23-18=5\).
- \(a_1=\left\lfloor 5/3\right\rfloor=1\), remainder \(5-3=2\).
- \(a_0=2\).

So
\[
293=(1\,0\,1\,2\,1\,2)_3=1\cdot 3^5+0\cdot 3^4+1\cdot 3^3+2\cdot 3^2+1\cdot 3^1+2\cdot 3^0.
\]

Therefore,
\[
293 = 1\cdot 3^5 + 0\cdot 3^4 + 1\cdot 3^3 + 2\cdot 3^2 + 1\cdot 3^1 + 2\cdot 3^0.
\]

### 3) Use digit-wise constraints for sums of \(\{0,1\}\)-coefficient ternary expansions
For any \(n\), \(f(n)\) has ternary digits only \(0\) or \(1\), because
\[
f(n)=\sum b_i 3^i \quad\text{with } b_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Let
\[
f(k)=\sum_{i\ge 0} x_i 3^i,\qquad f(l)=\sum_{i\ge 0} y_i 3^i,
\]
with \(x_i,y_i\in\{0,1\}\). Then
\[
f(k)+f(l)=\sum_{i\ge 0} (x_i+y_i)3^i=293.
\]
Since there is no carrying in base \(3\) only when \(x_i+y_i\in\{0,1,2\}\), and here the base-3 digits of \(293\) are indeed in \(\{0,1,2\}\), we can match digits directly:
\[
x_i+y_i = \text{(base-3 digit of }293\text{ at }3^i).
\]
From \(293=(1\,0\,1\,2\,1\,2)_3\), we read digits:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
i & 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 0\\ \hline
\text{digit at }3^i & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 2
\end{array}
\]
Thus:
- At \(i=5\): \(x_5+y_5=1\) \(\Rightarrow (x_5,y_5)=(1,0)\) or \((0,1)\).
- At \(i=4\): \(x_4+y_4=0\) \(\Rightarrow x_4=y_4=0\).
- At \(i=3\): \(x_3+y_3=1\) \(\Rightarrow (x_3,y_3)=(1,0)\) or \((0,1)\).
- At \(i=2\): \(x_2+y_2=2\) with \(x_2,y_2\in\{0,1\}\) \(\Rightarrow x_2=y_2=1\).
- At \(i=1\): \(x_1+y_1=1\) \(\Rightarrow (x_1,y_1)=(1,0)\) or \((0,1)\).
- At \(i=0\): \(x_0+y_0=2\) \(\Rightarrow x_0=y_0=1\).

So the only freedom is choosing, independently for \(i\in\{5,3,1\}\), which of \((k,l)\) gets the \(1\) digit in that position; digits at \(i=2\) and \(i=0\) must be \(1\) for both, and digit \(i=4\) must be \(0\) for both.

There are \(2^3=8\) ordered pairs \((f(k),f(l))\), and therefore up to swapping there will be \(4\) unordered pairs \(\{k,l\}\). The condition \(k<l\) will choose the ordering.

\[
[DEF]=k^2\cdot [\triangle(20,22,38)].

To make this explicit, apply **Heron’s formula** to the base triangle with sides \(20,22,38\).

Let
\[
s=\frac{20+22+38}{2}=\frac{80}{2}=40.

\[

=\sqrt{s(s-20)(s-22)(s-38)}
=\sqrt{40\cdot(40-20)\cdot(40-22)\cdot(40-38)}.

\[

\[
[\triangle(20,22,38)]

Multiply inside:
\[

\[

\[
\sqrt{28800}=\sqrt{36}\sqrt{8}\sqrt{100}=6\cdot 2\sqrt2 \cdot 10=120\sqrt2.

\[

Step 0: **Rewrite the ratio in a workable form and set up a maximization problem.**  
Let
\[
R=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(a_i+b_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n b_i(a_i+b_i)}.
\]
Using the given condition \(a_1+\cdots+a_n=b_1+\cdots+b_n>0\), we will later compare linear combinations of the terms \(a_i(a_i+b_i)\) and \(b_i(a_i+b_i)\). First, expand the numerator and denominator into a more explicit expression:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(a_i^2+a_i b_i\big)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i,
\]
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n b_i(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(b_i a_i+b_i^2\big)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i+\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
R=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)}.
\]
Now introduce the shorthand quantities
\[
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\quad B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,\quad C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i,
\]
so the ratio becomes the simplified expression
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}.
\]
At this point, the maximization task reduces to finding the largest possible value of \(\dfrac{A+C}{B+C}\) over all nonnegative \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) satisfying the given sum condition
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=:S>0.
\]
This is the setup we will use in the next step to bound \(R\) and determine its maximum.
Step 1: Using the shorthand from the previous step
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C},\quad A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\; B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,\; C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i,
\]
and the given condition (previous step premise) that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=:S>0,
\]
we next rewrite the ratio difference from a candidate value to turn the maximization into a sign condition.  

Let \(t\) be a real number. Then
\[
R\ge t \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{A+C}{B+C}\ge t.
\]
Since \(B+C=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\ge 0\) and we are assuming the denominator is positive because \(S>0\) and all terms are nonnegative, we may multiply both sides by \(B+C\) without changing the inequality direction:
\[
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\ge t
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
A+C \ge t(B+C).
\]
Now expand the right-hand side:
\[
A+C \ge tB+tC.
\]
Bring all terms to the left and regroup:
\[
A+C -tB -tC \ge 0
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
A - tB + (1-t)C \ge 0.
\]
Thus, for any \(t\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
R\ge t \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad A - tB + (1-t)C \ge 0.
\]
This converts the maximization of \(R\) into finding the largest \(t\) such that the inequality
\[
\boxed{A - tB + (1-t)C \ge 0}
\]
can hold for some nonnegative \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) with \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i=S>0\).

\[

\[

\frac{2+(1-t)}{2}a_i^2+\frac{-2t+(1-t)}{2}b_i^2
=
\frac{3-t}{2}a_i^2+\frac{1-3t}{2}b_i^2.
\]
Thus, pointwise,
\[
a_i^2 - tb_i^2 + (1-t)a_ib_i \le \frac{3-t}{2}a_i^2+\frac{1-3t}{2}b_i^2.
\]

Now sum this inequality over \(i=1,\dots,n\). Using the definitions of \(A=\sum a_i^2\), \(B=\sum b_i^2\), and \(C=\sum a_ib_i\), we obtain
\[
A-tB+(1-t)C \le \frac{3-t}{2}A+\frac{1-3t}{2}B.
\]
Rearrange to isolate \(A-tB+(1-t)C\) in terms of \(A,B\):
\[
A-tB+(1-t)C
\le
\frac{3-t}{2}A+\frac{1-3t}{2}B.
\]

This step sets up the next step: for a given \(t\), we will force \(A-tB+(1-t)C\ge 0\) (the condition for \(R\ge t\) from Step 1) by choosing the strongest possible bounds derived from \((a_i-b_i)^2\ge 0\) and the constraint \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i\).
Step 3: From Step 2 we have the equivalence
\[
R\ge t\quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad A-tB+(1-t)C\ge 0,
\]
where
\[
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\quad B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,\quad C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i,
\]
and the constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=:S>0\) with \(a_i,b_i\ge 0\).

However, the inequality derived in Step 2 is not yet a clean, correct upper/lower bound usable to determine the best \(t\). So in this Step 3 we correct the approach by switching to a standard **Cauchy-Schwarz bound** on \(C\), which is consistent with the given nonnegativity and the fixed sums.

### 1) Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to \(A,B\) and compare with \(C\)
By Cauchy-Schwarz,
\[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right),
\]
i.e.
\[
C^2 \le AB.
\]
Also, since \(a_i,b_i\ge 0\), we have \(C\ge 0\).

### 2) Convert the ratio to an inequality in \(t\)
Recall from Step 1:
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}.
\]
For a fixed \(t\), the condition \(R\ge t\) is equivalent to
\[
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\ge t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A+C \ge t(B+C).
\]
Rearrange:
\[
A+C \ge tB+tC
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A - tB + (1-t)C \ge 0.
\]
So for feasibility of \(R\ge t\), we need
\[
A - tB + (1-t)C \ge 0. \tag{*}
\]

### 3) Determine the maximal possible \(t\) by finding the worst-case (smallest LHS) using bounds on \(C\)
We want the largest \(t\) such that there exist nonnegative \(a_i,b_i\) with sums equal \(S\) making \((*)\) true.

Because \(C\ge 0\), the term \((1-t)C\) behaves differently depending on whether \(t\) is above or below \(1\):

- If \(t>1\), then \(1-t<0\), so \((1-t)C\) is **nonpositive**. To make \((*)\) hardest to satisfy, we should take \(C\) as **large as possible** (since it subtracts). The largest \(C\) given \(A,B\) occurs when equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds, i.e. when \((a_i)\) and \((b_i)\) are proportional, giving \(C=\sqrt{AB}\).

Thus, for \(t>1\), the minimal value of the left side for fixed \(A,B\) is achieved (worst case) at
\[
C=\sqrt{AB}.
\]
Substitute into the left side:
\[
A - tB + (1-t)C
\ge
A - tB + (1-t)\sqrt{AB}.
\]
Let \(x=\sqrt{A/B}\) (so \(A=x^2B\), with \(B>0\) since the total sum \(S>0\) and not all \(b_i\) are zero). Then
\[
A - tB + (1-t)\sqrt{AB}
=
x^2B - tB + (1-t)\sqrt{x^2B\cdot B}
=
B\Big(x^2 - t + (1-t)x\Big).
\]
So the condition \((*)\) becomes, in the worst case,
\[
B\Big(x^2 - t + (1-t)x\Big)\ge 0.
\]
Since \(B>0\), it reduces to
\[
x^2 + (1-t)x - t \ge 0. \tag{**}
\]

### 4) Enforce that (**) can hold for some \(x\ge 0\)
For (**) to be feasible, the quadratic
\[
f(x)=x^2+(1-t)x-t
\]
must have a nonnegative value for some \(x\ge 0\). The boundary (maximum feasible \(t\)) occurs when the quadratic just touches the axis, i.e. has discriminant \(0\):
\[
\Delta=(1-t)^2-4(1)(-t)=(1-t)^2+4t.
\]
Compute:
\[
(1-t)^2+4t=(1-2t+t^2)+4t=t^2+2t+1=(t+1)^2.
\]
So \(\Delta=(t+1)^2\), which is zero only if \(t=-1\). That would not match \(t>1\).

Therefore, for \(t>1\) the discriminant is always positive, meaning the inequality \(f(x)\ge 0\) can be satisfied only depending on the sign of roots and the allowed range of \(x\) imposed by the equal-sum constraint \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i=S\). At this point, Step 3 indicates we must incorporate the equal-sum condition to restrict \(x\); this will be done in the next step.

**Conclusion of Step 3 (setup for Step 4):** We have converted the maximization to a feasibility inequality
\[
A-tB+(1-t)C\ge 0,
\]
and for \(t>1\) reduced (via Cauchy-Schwarz) the worst-case to
\[
x^2+(1-t)x-t\ge 0,\quad x=\sqrt{A/B},
\]
but we must further use \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i\) to pin down the achievable range of \(x\) (which will yield the final maximal value of \(R\)).
Step 4: We now incorporate the missing piece: the constraint  
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=:S>0
\]
(which was not used correctly in Steps 3). We will determine the true maximum value of
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C},\quad A=\sum a_i^2,\;B=\sum b_i^2,\;C=\sum a_ib_i.
\]

**1) Reduce \(C\) using the vector proportionality that respects the constraint**

Let \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\) and \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\). For any fixed \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\),
\[
C=\langle \mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle.
\]
By Cauchy–Schwarz,
\[
C^2\le AB.
\]
Equality \(C=\sqrt{AB}\) holds iff \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) are proportional, i.e.
\[
\mathbf a=\lambda \mathbf b\quad (\lambda\ge 0).
\]
Now use the given sum constraint: if \(\mathbf a=\lambda\mathbf b\), then
\[
\sum a_i=\lambda\sum b_i \implies \lambda S=S\implies \lambda=1.
\]
So **under the equal-sum constraint**, the only proportional case is
\[
\mathbf a=\mathbf b \implies a_i=b_i\ \forall i,\quad\text{and then }C=\sqrt{AB}=A=B.
\]

We will show that the maximum of \(R\) indeed occurs at this proportional/equality case.

---

**2) Convert the maximization into a sharp inequality in \(A,B,C\)**

Starting from
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C},
\]
consider the inequality \(R\le t\) for some real \(t\). This is equivalent to
\[
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A+C\le t(B+C)
\]
(using \(B+C\ge 0\); and here \(B+C>0\) because \(S>0\) and not all \(b_i\) are zero). Thus
\[
A+C\le tB+tC
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A-tB+(1-t)C\le 0. \tag{1}
\]

So to find the **maximum** of \(R\), we look for the largest \(t\) such that (1) can hold for all admissible \((a_i,b_i)\), and we also seek equality cases.

---

**3) Use the equal-sum constraint to compare \(A\) and \(B\)**

By Cauchy–Schwarz,
\[
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \ge \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2}{n}=\frac{S^2}{n},
\]
and similarly
\[
B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2 \ge \frac{S^2}{n}.
\]
Also, because all \(a_i,b_i\ge 0\), we have \(C=\sum a_ib_i\ge 0\).

The key point is: since both \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) have the same sum \(S\), the best “alignment” to make \(R\) large is to make the numerator \(A+C\) large and the denominator \(B+C\) small. But \(B\) and \(A\) are tied together by the fixed sums: the smallest \(B\) for a given \(S\) occurs at uniform \(b_i\), and the smallest \(A\) for given \(S\) occurs at uniform \(a_i\). However, if we try to make \(A>B\) (to increase \(R\)), then the inner product \(C\) and the constraint structure force the denominator to increase correspondingly. The extremum is reached when the two vectors coincide.

To formalize that extremum, we check \(t=1\) first.

---

**4) Show \(R\le 1\) and find when equality holds**

We claim the maximum is \(1\). That is, we show
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le 1.
\]
This is equivalent to
\[
A+C \le B+C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\le B. \tag{2}
\]
So for \(R\le 1\) to be always true, we would need \(A\le B\) for all admissible pairs—which is not true. Hence the above direct approach fails.

So instead, we test the *candidate* equality case \(a_i=b_i\), and compute \(R\):
if \(a_i=b_i\) for all \(i\), then \(A=B\) and \(C=A\). Therefore
\[
R=\frac{A+A}{A+A}=1.
\]
So \(1\) is attainable.

Now we must show that no value \(>1\) is attainable.

Assume for contradiction that there exists admissible \((a_i,b_i)\) with \(R>1\). Then in (1) with \(t>1\),
\[
A-tB+(1-t)C\le 0
\]
must fail (since \(R>t\)). Take \(t=1+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\). Then (1) becomes
\[
A-(1+\varepsilon)B+(1-(1+\varepsilon))C\le 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A-(1+\varepsilon)B-\varepsilon C\le 0.
\]
Rearrange:
\[
A-B \le \varepsilon(B+C). \tag{3}
\]
Letting \(\varepsilon\to 0^+\), (3) would force
\[
A-B\le 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\le B.
\]
But if \(R>1\), then \(A+C>B+C\Rightarrow A>B\). That contradicts \(A\le B\).

Thus \(R>1\) is impossible, so
\[
R\le 1.
\]

Combining with attainability at \(a_i=b_i\), the maximum value is \(1\).

---

**5) Final answer**

Take \(a_i=b_i\) (any nonnegative choice not all zero, possible since \(n\ge 4\)). Then
\[
\frac{\sum a_i(a_i+b_i)}{\sum b_i(a_i+b_i)}=1.
\]
And we proved \(R\le 1\) for all admissible data. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
Step 5: We now complete the **extremal (sharp) construction** argument and finish **proving** the maximal value.

**Premises from previous steps:**  
From Step 1–2 we rewrote the ratio as
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C},
\quad
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\;B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,\;C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i,
\]
with \(a_i,b_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=:S>0\).  
From Step 4 we concluded the *candidate equality case* \(a_i=b_i\) gives \(R=1\), and we will now finish the **inequality** part properly to show **no** \(R>1\) is possible.

---

### 5.1 Construct an equality case (attainment of the bound)
Choose any nonnegative numbers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) not all zero and set
\[
a_i=b_i=x_i\quad (i=1,\dots,n).
\]
Then automatically
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i =:S>0.
\]
Compute:
\[
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2,
\quad
B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2=A,
\]
and
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\cdot x_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2=A.
\]
Therefore
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}=\frac{A+A}{A+A}=1.
\]
So the maximum is **at least**
\[
R_{\max}\ge 1.
\]

---

### 5.2 Prove the sharp inequality \(R\le 1\)
To prove \(R\le 1\), we use that \(B+C>0\). Indeed, since \(S>0\) and all terms are nonnegative, not all \(b_i\) are zero, hence
\[
B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2>0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
B+C\ge B>0.
\]

Now start from the definition:
\[
R\le 1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le 1.
\]
Because \(B+C>0\), we can multiply without changing the inequality direction:
\[
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le 1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A+C\le B+C.
\]
Subtract \(C\) from both sides:
\[
A+C\le B+C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\le B.
\]
Thus,
\[
R\le 1 \quad\text{is equivalent to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2.
\]
So we need to show \(A\le B\) always holds under the condition \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i\) and \(R>1\) is impossible.

Assume for contradiction that \(R>1\) for some admissible \((a_i,b_i)\). Then
\[
\frac{A+C}{B+C}>1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A+C>B+C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A>B. \tag{1}
\]
Now use the standard identity (valid for all real \(a_i,b_i\)):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-b_i)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2-2\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i
=
A+B-2C.
\]
Since \((a_i-b_i)^2\ge 0\),
\[
A+B-2C \ge 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A+B \ge 2C. \tag{2}
\]

Next, recall we have the fixed-sum condition \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i=S\). Expand:
\[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\right)^2=0.
\]
But
\[
\left(\sum a_i-\sum b_i\right)^2
=
\left(\sum a_i\right)^2+\left(\sum b_i\right)^2-2\left(\sum a_i\right)\left(\sum b_i\right)
= S^2+S^2-2S^2=0,
\]
which is an identity and does not further constrain \(A,B,C\). So we proceed directly with (1) and (2).

From (1), \(A>B\). Add \(B\) to both sides:
\[
A+B > 2B.
\]
Combine with (2):
\[
A+B \ge 2C
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2C \le A+B.
\]
But if \(A>B\), then the ratio \(\frac{A+C}{B+C}\) exceeds \(1\) only when the numerator “gains” relative to the denominator; the extremal alignment for such gain under the nonnegativity and symmetric definition of \(A,B,C\) occurs at \(a_i=b_i\), where \(A=B\). Since our contradiction assumption enforces \(A>B\), it violates the equality condition for the nonnegative quadratic extremum (namely, \(\sum (a_i-b_i)^2=0\) occurs exactly at \(a_i=b_i\), giving \(A=B\)).

Concretely, if \(R>1\), then \(A>B\) by (1), hence
\[
A-B>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(A-B)^2>0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-b_i)^2>0,
\]
so \(a_i\ne b_i\) for some \(i\). But then the symmetric construction that maximizes \(\frac{A+C}{B+C}\) forces \(a_i=b_i\) (otherwise the Cauchy-Schwarz/Chebyshev-type alignment that makes \(C\) large relative to \(A,B\) is not simultaneously compatible with the fixed total sums). Therefore \(R>1\) cannot occur.

Hence,
\[
R\le 1.
\]

---

### 5.3 Finish (sharp maximum)
We have shown:
- \(R=1\) is achievable by \(a_i=b_i\).
- No configuration can yield \(R>1\).

Therefore the maximum is
\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
Step 6: **Finish the proof rigorously: show \(R\le 1\) for all admissible \((a_i,b_i)\) and identify equality.**

From Step 1 we have the shorthand
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C},
\qquad
A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\; B=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,\; C=\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i,
\]
with \(a_i,b_i\ge 0\) and \(S:=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i>0\).
Also \(B+C>0\) because \(S>0\) implies not all \(b_i\) are zero, hence \(B=\sum b_i^2>0\).

### 1) Reduce the claim \(R\le 1\) to an inequality in \(A,B\)
We claim \(R\le 1\). Since \(B+C>0\),
\[
R\le 1
\Longleftrightarrow
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le 1
\Longleftrightarrow
A+C\le B+C
\Longleftrightarrow
A\le B.
\]
So it suffices to prove:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2. \tag{1}
\]

### 2) Use the fixed-sum condition to force \(A\le B\)
Consider the nonnegative quantity
\[
0\le \sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-b_i)(a_i+b_i).
\]
Using the algebraic identity (valid for every real pair \((x,y)\)):
\[
(x-y)(x+y)=x^2-y^2,
\]
we get term-by-term:
\[
(a_i-b_i)(a_i+b_i)=a_i^2-b_i^2.
\]
Summing over \(i=1,\dots,n\),
\[
0\le \sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-b_i)(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i^2-b_i^2)=A-B. \tag{2}
\]
Thus (2) gives
\[
A-B\ge 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\ge B,
\]
which is the *opposite* direction of (1). Therefore, the attempted reduction in Step 5 (“\(R\le 1\) iff \(A\le B\) and always \(A\le B\)”) cannot be correct as stated.

### 3) Correct direction and finish maximization
Instead, we compute the actual inequality direction directly from the expression for \(R\).
Assume we want an upper bound \(R\le t\). From Step 1,
\[
R\le t
\Longleftrightarrow
\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le t
\Longleftrightarrow
A+C\le tB+tC
\Longleftrightarrow
A-tB+(1-t)C\le 0. \tag{3}
\]

Now take the candidate value \(t=1\). Then (3) becomes
\[
A-1\cdot B+(1-1)C\le 0
\Longleftrightarrow
A-B\le 0
\Longleftrightarrow
A\le B.
\]
But from (2) we have \(A-B\ge 0\). Hence for \(t=1\),
\[
A\le B \text{ and } A\ge B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=B.
\]
Therefore \(R\le 1\) is equivalent to the *rigid* condition \(A=B\), i.e. \(\sum a_i^2=\sum b_i^2\).

### 4) Determine the true maximum value by exhibiting a configuration
We can make \(R>1\) by choosing \(a_i\) larger than \(b_i\) in squares while keeping \(\sum a_i=\sum b_i\).
For example, let \(n\ge 4\) and define (with \(S=1\)):
\[
a_1=1,\ a_2=a_3=a_4=\cdots=a_n=0,
\]
\[
b_1=b_2=\frac12,\quad b_3=b_4=\cdots=b_n=0.
\]
Then \(\sum a_i=1\) and \(\sum b_i=\frac12+\frac12=1\), so the condition holds.
Compute:
\[
A=\sum a_i^2=1^2+0+\cdots+0=1,
\]
\[
B=\sum b_i^2=\left(\frac12\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12,

\[
C=\sum a_ib_i=a_1b_1=1\cdot \frac12=\frac12
\]
(since all other \(a_i\) are \(0\)).
Thus
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}=\frac{1+\frac12}{\frac12+\frac12}=\frac{\frac32}{1}=\frac32.
\]
So \(R\) can be at least \(\frac32\). In particular, \(R_{\max}\neq 1\).

is achievable.

### 7.2 A universal upper bound using Cauchy–Schwarz with the fixed sum
We use Cauchy–Schwarz in the form
\[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i^2}{b_i+b_i^2/(a_i+b_i)}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \left(b_i+\frac{b_i^2}{a_i}\right)\right),

but that is messy. Instead, use a clean standard inequality that directly relates \(A,B,C\).

Consider
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-b_i)^2 \ge 0

which expands to
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i^2+b_i^2-2a_ib_i)\ge 0

A+B-2C\ge 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2C\le A+B.
\tag{1}

Also, the fixed sum gives by Cauchy–Schwarz:
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \le \sqrt{n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2}=\sqrt{nA}

and similarly
\[
B\ge \frac{S^2}{n}.
\tag{2}

Now we need an inequality in \(A,B,C\) that bounds \(\dfrac{A+C}{B+C}\).

\[
C \le \frac{A+B}{2}.
\]
Then
\[
A+C \le A+\frac{A+B}{2}=\frac{3A+B}{2},
\]
and
\[
B+C \ge B+0=B.
\]
So for all admissible nonnegative data,
\[
R=\frac{A+C}{B+C}\le \frac{\frac{3A+B}{2}}{B}=\frac{3A+B}{2B}=\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{A}{B}+\frac{1}{2}.
\tag{3}
\]
This still depends on \(\frac{A}{B}\). So we must bound \(\frac{A}{B}\) using the fixed-sum structure.

### 7.3 Show \(\frac{A}{B}\le \frac{1}{1}\) is false; instead determine the sharp extremum by construction

### 7.4 Prove \(C \ge 2A-3B\) via pointwise quadratic inequality
Fix an index \(i\). We will prove the pointwise inequality
\[
a_i b_i \ge 2a_i^2-3b_i^2

and then sum over \(i\).

To verify (7), rearrange it as

To minimize an LCM, we want both \(k_A\) and \(k_B\) to be as small as possible, i.e. we want \(\***(180,n)\) and \(\***(180,n+1)\) as large as possible.

Factor
\[
180 = 2^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5.
\]

We try to make \(n\) share large common factors with \(180\) and simultaneously \(n+1\) share large common factors with \(180\). The best possible is to make both gcds as large as possible, but since \(n\) and \(n+1\) are consecutive, they cannot share the same prime factor.

A strong candidate is to make:
- \(\***(180,n)\) large using prime factors from \(180\),
- \(\***(180,n+1)\) large using the remaining prime factors.

Take \(n=44\) (which is within \(1\) to \(89\)):

  Hence
  \[

Now \(n+1=45\):
- \(\***(180,45)\):
  \[
  180=45\cdot 4 \implies \***(180,45)=45.
  \]
  Hence
  \[
  k_B=\frac{180}{45}=4.

\[

\[

\]
Because \(g\) is a bijection, we can cancel \(g\) to get
\[

\]
which contradicts \(x\in C_f\) (where \(f(x)\neq x\)).  

Therefore, \(g(x)\in C_f\). Since \(x\in C_f\) was arbitrary, we conclude:
\[
g(C_f)\subseteq C_f.
\]
Because \(g\) is a bijection on the finite set \(S\), this containment implies equality:
\[
g(C_f)=C_f.
\]

Similarly, by swapping roles of \(f\) and \(g\), we obtain
\[
f(C_g)=C_g.
\]

\[
|C_f|=|g(C_f)|=|C_f\cap C_g| \ \text{(in fact the entire cycles coincide)}.
\]

\[

### Case 1: \(c=0\)
Then \(b+2c=b\equiv 0\pmod 3\), so \(b\in\{0,3\}\) (and also \(b+c=b\le 5\)).
- If \(b=0\), then \(a=5-b-c=5-0-0=5\). Triple: \((a,b,c)=(5,0,0)\).
- If \(b=3\), then \(a=5-3-0=2\). Triple: \((a,b,c)=(2,3,0)\).

### Case 2: \(c=1\)
Then \(b+2c=b+2\equiv 0\pmod 3\), so \(b\equiv -2\equiv 1\pmod 3\). Thus \(b\in\{1,4\}\) (and \(b+c=b+1\le 5\)).
- If \(b=1\), then \(a=5-1-1=3\). Triple: \((3,1,1)\).
- If \(b=4\), then \(a=5-4-1=0\). Triple: \((0,4,1)\).

### Case 3: \(c=2\)
Then \(b+2c=b+4\equiv 0\pmod 3\). Since \(4\equiv 1\pmod 3\), this is \(b+1\equiv 0\pmod 3\), so \(b\equiv -1\equiv 2\pmod 3\). Thus \(b\in\{2\}\) (since \(b+c=b+2\le 5\)).
- If \(b=2\), then \(a=5-2-2=1\). Triple: \((1,2,2)\).

### Case 4: \(c=3\)
Then \(b+2c=b+6\equiv 0\pmod 3\). Since \(6\equiv 0\pmod 3\), we get \(b\equiv 0\pmod 3\). So \(b\in\{0,3\}\), but also \(b+c=b+3\le 5\), hence \(b\le 2\).
- The only possibility is \(b=0\). Then \(a=5-0-3=2\). Triple: \((2,0,3)\).

### Case 5: \(c=4\)
Then \(b+2c=b+8\equiv 0\pmod 3\). Since \(8\equiv 2\pmod 3\), this is \(b+2\equiv 0\pmod 3\), so \(b\equiv 1\pmod 3\).
But \(b+c=b+4\le 5\) forces \(b\le 1\), so \(b=1\) is the only option.
- If \(b=1\), then \(a=5-1-4=0\). Triple: \((0,1,4)\).

### Case 6: \(c=5\)
Then \(b+2c=b+10\equiv 0\pmod 3\). Since \(10\equiv 1\pmod 3\), we get \(b+1\equiv 0\pmod 3\), so \(b\equiv 2\pmod 3\).
But \(b+c=b+5\le 5\) forces \(b=0\), which is not congruent to \(2\pmod 3\).  
So there are **no** valid triples for \(c=5\).

### Valid residue-count triples
Collecting all solutions \((a,b,c)\) with \(a+b+c=5\) and \(b+2c\equiv 0\pmod 3\), we have:
\[
(5,0,0),\ (2,3,0),\ (3,1,1),\ (0,4,1),\ (1,2,2),\ (2,0,3),\ (0,1,4).
\]
We will use these in the next step to compute the number of 5-element selections (subsets) that realize each triple, using the fact from Step 1 that each residue class has exactly \(5\) available numbers.

\[

- \(x_My_E=\left(-\frac a2\right)v=-\frac{av}{2}\)
- \(x_Ey_D=0\cdot \frac v2=0\)

\[

\]

- \(y_Dx_I=\left(\frac v2\right)\cdot 0=0\)
- \(y_Ix_M=u\left(-\frac a2\right)=-\frac{au}{2}\)
- \(y_Mx_E=\left(\frac v2\right)\cdot 0=0\)
- \(y_Ex_D=v\left(\frac a2\right)=\frac{av}{2}\)

\[

\]

Subtract:
\[
\sum x_i y_{i+1}-\sum y_i x_{i+1}
=\frac{a(u-v)}{2}-\frac{a(v-u)}{2}
=\frac{a(u-v)}{2}-\left(-\frac{a(u-v)}{2}\right)

\]

Step 0: We set up coordinates and interpret the grid geometry precisely so that later we can use invariants/counting to restrict which Hamiltonian (210-vertex, non-selfintersecting) polygons are possible and how their areas can vary.

1. **Understand the triangular grid \(G\).**  
   The grid has \(20\) points on each side of an equilateral triangular arrangement, with rows of points:
   \[
   1,2,3,\dots,20
   \]
   points per row. The total number of points is therefore
   \[
   1+2+\cdots+20=\frac{20\cdot 21}{2}=210,
   \]
   matching the statement “there are 210 points.”

2. **Choose a coordinate system consistent with unit spacing.**  
   Place the grid in the plane using an equilateral-triangle lattice with side-length (row spacing) \(1\). A standard coordinate model uses “horizontal” rows:
   - Let row \(r\) (with \(r=1,2,\dots,20\)) contain \(r\) points.
   - Within each row, consecutive points are \(1\) unit apart horizontally.
   - Adjacent rows are shifted by half a unit so that the overall lattice consists of equilateral triangles of side \(1\).

   Concretely, let the vertical separation between consecutive rows be \(\frac{\sqrt 3}{2}\) (the height of an equilateral triangle of side \(1\)).  
   Then we can assign coordinates as follows: for each row \(r\), and each point index \(j=1,2,\dots,r\),
   \[
   (x_{r,j},y_{r,j})=\left(j-1,\ (r-1)\cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),
   \]
   and interpret the “missing” points in shorter rows as not belonging to the set.  
   This coordinate choice makes the distance between adjacent points in the same row equal to \(1\), and ensures the row-to-row structure corresponds to equilateral triangles.

3. **Reduce the problem to “area of a polygon through all lattice points.”**  
   The polygon \(S\) is:
   - closed,
   - non-selfintersecting,
   - uses each of the \(210\) grid points exactly once (so it is a Hamiltonian cycle on the induced point set in this triangular-grid geometry),

\boxed{R^2\sqrt3\sin\frac{x}{2}\cdot \sin\left(60^\circ+\frac{x}{2}\right)=3.}
\]

Use the trig identity
\[
\sin\left(60^\circ+\frac{x}{2}\right)=\sin60^\circ\cos\frac{x}{2}+\cos60^\circ\sin\frac{x}{2}
=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}+\frac12\sin\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Let \(t=\sin\frac{x}{2}\) and \(u=\cos\frac{x}{2}\) with \(u^2+t^2=1\). Then
\[
\sin\left(60^\circ+\frac{x}{2}\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}u+\frac12 t.
\]
Hence
\[
3 = R^2\sqrt3\cdot t\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}u+\frac12 t\right)
= R^2\sqrt3\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}tu+\frac12 t^2\right).
\]
Compute \(\sqrt3\cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\):
\[
3 = R^2\left(\frac{3}{2}tu+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}t^2\right).
\]
Multiply both sides by \(2\):
\[
6 = R^2\left(3tu+\sqrt3\,t^2\right).
\]
So
\[
\boxed{R^2=\frac{6}{3tu+\sqrt3\,t^2}.}
\]

### 5.4 Express \([ACD]\) in terms of \(R\) and \(x\)
We are given \([ACD]=4\).

In \(\triangle ACD\),
\[
AC = R\sqrt3
\]
(same chord as \(AB\)).

Also
\[
AD = 2R\sin\left(\frac{\angle AOD}{2}\right)=2R\sin\frac{x}{2}=2Rt.
\]

The included angle \(\angle CAD\) is an inscribed angle subtending arc \(CD\). The central angle \(\angle COD\) equals
\[
\angle COD = 120^\circ - x
\]
because from \(OC\) to \(OA\) is \(120^\circ\), and \(OD\) is \(x\) away from \(OA\) toward \(OB\). Thus
\[
\angle CAD = \frac12\angle COD = \frac12(120^\circ-x)=60^\circ-\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
[ACD]=\frac12\cdot AC\cdot AD\cdot \sin(\angle CAD)
=\frac12\cdot (R\sqrt3)\cdot (2Rt)\cdot \sin\left(60^\circ-\frac{x}{2}\right).
\]
Simplify:
\[
[ACD]= R^2\sqrt3\, t\cdot \sin\left(60^\circ-\frac{x}{2}\right).
\]
Use
\[
\sin\left(60^\circ-\frac{x}{2}\right)=\sin60^\circ\cos\frac{x}{2}-\cos60^\circ\sin\frac{x}{2}
=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}u-\frac12 t.
\]
So
\[
4 = R^2\sqrt3\, t\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}u-\frac12 t\right)
= R^2\sqrt3\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}tu-\frac12 t^2\right)
=R^2\left(\frac{3}{2}tu-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}t^2\right).
\]
Multiply by \(2\):
\[
8 = R^2\left(3tu-\sqrt3\,t^2\right).
\]
So
\[
\boxed{R^2=\frac{8}{3tu-\sqrt3\,t^2}.}
\]

### 5.5 Eliminate \(R^2\) to solve for \(tu\) and \(t^2\)
Set the two expressions for \(R^2\) equal:
\[
\frac{6}{3tu+\sqrt3\,t^2}=\frac{8}{3tu-\sqrt3\,t^2}.
\]
Cross-multiply:
\[
6(3tu-\sqrt3\,t^2)=8(3tu+\sqrt3\,t^2).
\]
Expand both sides:
\[
18tu-6\sqrt3\,t^2=24tu+8\sqrt3\,t^2.
\]
Bring like terms together. Subtract \(18tu\) from both sides:
\[
-6\sqrt3\,t^2=6tu+8\sqrt3\,t^2.
\]
Add \(6\sqrt3\,t^2\) to both sides:
\[
0=6tu+14\sqrt3\,t^2.
\]
Divide by \(2\):
\[
0=3tu+7\sqrt3\,t^2.
\]
So
\[
3tu=-7\sqrt3\,t^2.
\]
If \(t=0\) then \(AE=0\) would be degenerate, impossible; hence \(t\neq 0\). Divide by \(t\):
\[
3u=-7\sqrt3\,t.
\]
Thus
\[
u=\,-\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}t.
\]
Use \(u^2+t^2=1\):
\[
\left(-\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}t\right)^2+t^2=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{147}{9}t^2+t^2=1.
\]
Compute \(\frac{147}{9}=\frac{49}{3}\):
\[
\frac{49}{3}t^2+t^2=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\left(\frac{49}{3}+\frac{3}{3}\right)t^2=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{52}{3}t^2=1.
\]
Hence
\[
t^2=\frac{3}{52}.
\]
Then
\[
u^2=1-t^2=1-\frac{3}{52}=\frac{49}{52}.
\]
So
\[
tu = \pm \sqrt{t^2u^2}=\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{52}\cdot\frac{49}{52}}
=\pm \sqrt{\frac{147}{2704}}=\pm \frac{\sqrt{147}}{52}
=\pm \frac{7\sqrt3}{52}.
\]
But from \(u=-\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}t\), the signs satisfy \(tu<0\), so
\[
tu = -\frac{7\sqrt3}{52}.
\]

Step 0: **Set up the random experiment and identify the quantity to count.**

Paul independently creates **two** random arrangements of the numbers \(1,2,\dots,49\) in a \(7\times 7\) grid. Fix these two arrangements and call them Arrangement A and Arrangement B.

For each arrangement separately, consider **unordered pairs** of distinct numbers \(\{a,b\}\) (where \(1\le a<b\le 49\)).  
For Arrangement A, define the event
\[
E_A(a,b):\quad \text{“\(a\) and \(b\) are in the same row or the same column in Arrangement A.”}
\]
Similarly for Arrangement B,
\[
E_B(a,b):\quad \text{“\(a\) and \(b\) are in the same row or the same column in Arrangement B.”}
\]

The problem asks for the **expected number of pairs \(\{a,b\}\)** such that **both arrangements simultaneously** have the pair in the same row/column:
\[
E_A(a,b)\ \text{and}\ E_B(a,b)\ \text{both occur.}
\]

So define the random variable \(X\) to be
\[
X=\#\Big\{\{a,b\}:1\le a<b\le 49,\ \big(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b)\big)\Big\}.
\]

We will compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) using **linearity of expectation** by expressing \(X\) as a sum of indicator variables:
for each pair \(\{a,b\}\), let
\[
I_{a,b}=
\begin{cases}
1,& \text{if }E_A(a,b)\text{ and }E_B(a,b)\text{ both occur},\\
0,& \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Then, by definition of \(X\) as a count,
\[
X=\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49} I_{a,b}.
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49} I_{a,b}\right].
\]
Using linearity of expectation (this is the key “linearity” principle),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49}\mathbb{E}[I_{a,b}].
\]

Since \(I_{a,b}\) is an indicator,
\[
\mathbb{E}[I_{a,b}]=\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b)).
\]

Next step (Step 1) will compute \(\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))\) for a fixed pair \(\{a,b\}\), using the symmetry of random arrangements and the independence of Arrangements A and B.
Step 2: **Compute \(\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))\) for a fixed unordered pair \(\{a,b\}\).**

**Premises used:**  
From Step 1, we will sum \(\mathbb{E}[I_{a,b}]=\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))\) over all unordered pairs \(\{a,b\}\) with \(1\le a<b\le 49\), and Arrangements A and B are independent random arrangements of the same \(7\times 7\) grid.

---

### 2.1 Probability in a single arrangement
Fix an unordered pair of distinct numbers \(\{a,b\}\). Consider **one** random arrangement (say Arrangement A). In the \(7\times 7\) grid there are \(49\) cells total.

- The number \(a\) is equally likely to be in any of the \(49\) cells.
- Given the cell of \(a\), the number \(b\) is equally likely to be in any of the remaining \(48\) cells.

So we compute \(\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b))\) by classifying which positions for \(b\) make \(a\) and \(b\) lie in the same **row or column**.

**Geometry of the \(7\times 7\) grid (key count):**
- If \(b\) is in the **same row** as \(a\): there are \(6\) other cells in that row.
- If \(b\) is in the **same column** as \(a\): there are \(6\) other cells in that column.
- The intersection (same row AND same column) would mean the same cell, which is impossible because \(b\neq a\).
  So we can add without overlap.

Thus, for a fixed location of \(a\), the number of “good” cells for \(b\) is
\[
6+6=12.
\]
Since \(b\) has \(48\) possible remaining cells,
\[
\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b))=\frac{12}{48}=\frac{1}{4}.
\]

---

### 2.2 Use independence between arrangements A and B
From the problem statement, Paul creates the two arrangements **independently**. Therefore, the events
\[
E_A(a,b)\quad \text{and}\quad E_B(a,b)
\]
are independent (they depend on disjoint randomness: Arrangement A vs. Arrangement B).

So,
\[
\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))
=\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b))\cdot \mathbb{P}(E_B(a,b)).
\]

But by symmetry of the random arrangement,
\[
\mathbb{P}(E_B(a,b))=\frac{1}{4}.
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))
=\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}
=\frac{1}{16}.
\]

---

### 2.3 Result for the fixed pair
For every fixed unordered pair \(\{a,b\}\) with \(1\le a<b\le 49\),
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b))=\frac{1}{16}}.
\]

This value will be substituted in the expectation sum from Step 1 in Step 3.
Step 4: **Sum the probabilities over all unordered pairs \(\{a,b\}\) to get \(\mathbb{E}[X]\).**

From **Step 1**, we defined the random variable
\[
X=\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49} I_{a,b},
\]
so by linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49}\mathbb{E}[I_{a,b}]
=\sum_{1\le a<b\le 49}\Pr\!\big(E_A(a,b)\cap E_B(a,b)\big).
\]

Step 0: Model the situation as a bipartite graph: put the girls \(G_1,\dots,G_n\) on one side and the boys \(B_1,\dots,B_n\) on the other side, and draw an edge between \(G_i\) and \(B_j\) exactly when the pair \((G_i,B_j)\) is suitable (i.e., when girl \(G_i\) is willing to marry boy \(B_j\)). The given condition says there is **exactly one** way to pair each girl with a **distinct** boy that she is willing to marry; in graph terms, this means there is **exactly one perfect matching** in this bipartite graph. Let \(E\) be the set of suitable pairs (edges). Then the **maximal possible number of suitable pairs** is the maximal possible value of \(|E|\) among all bipartite graphs with exactly one perfect matching. We now proceed to determine this maximum.
Step 1: From the previous step’s model (bipartite graph with girls on one side, boys on the other, and an edge for each suitable pair), use the given premise: **there is exactly one perfect matching** that pairs every girl with a distinct boy she is willing to marry. Let \(E\) be the set of suitable pairs (edges), and let \(|E|\) be the number of suitable pairs. Since a perfect matching has size \(n\), this implies **at least** \(n\) edges are needed (because every girl \(G_i\) must be incident to at least one edge in order for a matching to cover all \(n\) girls). Hence, with only edges required for the existence of a perfect matching, we have the basic bound
\[
|E|\ge n.
\]
We will use the stronger structural constraint coming from **uniqueness** of the perfect matching in the next step to determine the maximal possible value of \(|E|\).
Step 2: Use the premise from Step 1 (“there is exactly one perfect matching, of size \(n\)”) to derive an upper bound on the number of edges \(|E|\), hence on the number of suitable pairs.

Let \(G\) be the bipartite graph with bipartition \(\{G_1,\dots,G_n\}\) and \(\{B_1,\dots,B_n\}\), and let \(E\) be the set of edges (suitable pairs). By the given condition (“exactly one way to pair each girl with a distinct boy that she is willing to marry”), there exists a unique perfect matching \(M\). Therefore:

- Every girl \(G_i\) is incident to at least one edge in \(E\) (otherwise she could not be matched in any perfect matching). This is exactly the premise used in Step 1, so we already have \(|E|\ge n\).
- Now we strengthen using **uniqueness**: suppose for contradiction that \(|E|\) is “too large.” Consider the structure of the edges around the unique perfect matching \(M\).

Let \(M\) pair each \(G_i\) with exactly one boy; denote the matched boy by \(f(i)\), so \((G_i,B_{f(i)})\in M\). Since \(M\) is a perfect matching, we have exactly \(n\) edges in \(M\).

Next, consider any girl \(G_i\). If she has an edge to some boy \(B_j\neq B_{f(i)}\), i.e. if \((G_i,B_j)\in E\setminus M\), then we can attempt to build an alternative perfect matching. The only way uniqueness can still hold is if adding \((G_i,B_j)\) necessarily “blocks” all attempts to rearrange the matching. In bipartite graphs, the standard obstruction mechanism for alternative perfect matchings is the presence/absence of alternating cycles:  

- Any alternative perfect matching differing from \(M\) must be obtainable by switching along an **\(M\)-alternating cycle** (edges alternate between not-in-\(M\) and in-\(M\)).  
- Therefore, uniqueness of the perfect matching is equivalent to saying: there are **no \(M\)-alternating cycles** in \(G\). (Otherwise, switching along such a cycle produces a different perfect matching.)

Now we use this cycle-free consequence to bound the number of non-matching edges. Construct a directed graph on the matched edges: for each non-matching edge \((G_i,B_j)\in E\setminus M\), create a directed edge from the matched boy of \(G_i\) to the matched boy associated with \(B_j\)’s partner under \(M\). Concretely, since \(M\) matches exactly one girl to each boy, there is a unique index \(k\) such that \(B_j\) is matched to \(G_k\), i.e. \(B_j=B_{f(k)}\). Thus each non-matching edge \((G_i,B_j)\) corresponds to a directed edge
\[
f(i)\to f(k).
\]
Under this construction, an \(M\)-alternating cycle in the original bipartite graph corresponds exactly to a directed cycle in the directed graph. Since uniqueness forbids alternating cycles, the directed graph must be **acyclic**.

An acyclic directed graph on \(n\) vertices has at most \(\binom{n}{2}\) directed edges (because the maximum number of edges in a DAG is achieved by a total ordering where every edge goes “forward,” giving \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\)). Hence the number of non-matching edges satisfies
\[
|E\setminus M|\le \binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]

Finally, since \(|M|=n\) and \(E\) is the disjoint union \(M\cup (E\setminus M)\), we get
\[
|E|=|M|+|E\setminus M|\le n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]
Compute the right-hand side:
\[
n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
=\frac{2n}{2}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
=\frac{2n+n(n-1)}{2}
=\frac{n(n-1)+2n}{2}
=\frac{n(n-1+2)}{2}
=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]

Thus, using the uniqueness of the perfect matching (no alternating cycles) and the acyclic bound on the resulting directed graph, we obtain the upper bound
\[
|E|\le \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]

(We have not yet shown this bound is achievable; that will be the goal of the next step.)
Step 3: **(Achievability / construction)** We have proved in the previous steps that any bipartite graph with exactly one perfect matching \(M\) satisfies the upper bound
\[
|E|\le \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]
It remains to show this bound is **maximal**, i.e. that there exists a configuration with exactly one perfect matching whose number of suitable pairs equals \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\).

Let the unique perfect matching \(M\) be
\[
M=\{(G_i,B_i)\mid i=1,2,\dots,n\}.
\]
We will define the set \(E\) of suitable pairs as follows:

- Include all matching edges: for each \(i\), include \((G_i,B_i)\).
- Additionally include every “upper-triangular” non-matching edge:
  \[
  (G_i,B_j)\in E \quad \text{whenever } 1\le i<j\le n.
  \]
- Do **not** include any “lower-triangular” non-matching edge:
  \[
  (G_i,B_j)\notin E \quad \text{whenever } 1\le j<i\le n.
  \]

Now we verify two facts: (i) the perfect matching is unique, and (ii) the edge count hits the bound.

---

### (i) Uniqueness of the perfect matching
Suppose there were a different perfect matching \(M'\neq M\). Any other perfect matching must differ from \(M\) on some edges. In a bipartite graph, the symmetric difference \(M\triangle M'\) decomposes into disjoint alternating cycles (edges alternate between \(M\) and \(M'\)). Therefore, if \(M'\neq M\) exists, then there is an \(M\)-alternating cycle.

So it suffices to show: **there is no \(M\)-alternating cycle** in our constructed graph.

Consider the directed graph method used in the previous steps: define a directed edge for each non-matching edge \((G_i,B_j)\in E\setminus M\) from the matched boy of \(G_i\) to the matched boy of \(G_k\), where \(B_j\) is matched in \(M\) with \(G_k\). In our construction, matched partners in \(M\) are
\[
B_t \text{ is matched to } G_t.
\]
Thus, for a non-matching edge with \(i<j\),
\[
(G_i,B_j)\in E\setminus M,
\]
the corresponding directed edge goes
\[
f(i)\to f(k)\quad \text{where } f(i)=i,\ f(k)=j.
\]
Hence it becomes
\[
i\to j.
\]
But because we included non-matching edges only when \(i<j\), **every directed edge satisfies \(i<j\)**. Therefore, there cannot be a directed cycle (a directed cycle would require some edge that eventually decreases an index, contradicting all edges going strictly “forward”).

So there are **no** \(M\)-alternating cycles, which implies there is **exactly one** perfect matching, namely \(M\).

---

### (ii) Counting suitable pairs
We count \(|E|\).

- Matching edges: \((G_i,B_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,n\). That contributes \(n\) edges.
- Non-matching edges: we included \((G_i,B_j)\) for every pair \((i,j)\) with \(1\le i<j\le n\). The number of such pairs is
  \[
  \binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
  \]

Therefore,
\[
|E|=n+\binom{n}{2}
= n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
= \frac{2n}{2}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
= \frac{2n+n(n-1)}{2}
= \frac{2n+n^2-n}{2}
= \frac{n^2+n}{2}
= \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]

---

Since we constructed a bipartite graph with exactly one perfect matching and exactly \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) suitable pairs, this matches the upper bound from Step 2. Hence the maximal possible number of suitable pairs is exactly \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\), which we will box in the next step.
Step 4: **Achievability (construction) and final count**

From the argument in **Step 3**, uniqueness of the perfect matching is equivalent to having **no \(M\)-alternating cycle**; otherwise one could perform a “swapping along” an alternating cycle to obtain a second perfect matching.

In this construction, every **additional** non-matching edge \((G_i,B_j)\) with \(i<j\) points “forward” in index. Under the directed-cycle interpretation from Step 3, any directed edge created from a non-matching edge goes from index \(i\) to index \(j\) with

\]
Therefore, it is impossible to form a directed cycle (each step strictly increases the index), so there is **no** directed cycle and hence **no** \(M\)-alternating cycle. Thus the perfect matching \(M\) is **unique**.

So our construction satisfies the given premise: **exactly one perfect matching**.

---

### 3) Count the number of suitable pairs \(|E|\)
We now compute \(|E|\) in this construction.

**(a) Matching edges:** there are exactly \(n\) edges:
\[
\#(M)=n.
\]

**(b) Non-matching edges:** we included all \((G_i,B_j)\) with \(1\le i<j\le n\). The number of such pairs is the binomial coefficient
\[
\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]

Therefore,
\[
|E| = n+\binom{n}{2}
= n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]
Put everything over denominator \(2\):
\[
|E|
= \frac{2n}{2}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
= \frac{2n+n(n-1)}{2}.
\]
Expand \(n(n-1)\):
\[
|E|
= \frac{2n+(n^2-n)}{2}
= \frac{2n+n^2-n}{2}
= \frac{n^2+n}{2}
= \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]

So the number of suitable pairs in our explicit construction is
\[
|E|=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]

---

### 4) Conclude maximality
By **Step 3**, no graph can exceed \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\). By this construction, \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) is achievable. Hence this value is maximal.

\[
\boxed{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}
\]

### 4.3. The key “halving” invariant
Define
\[
u_i:=S_i \quad\text{(George’s running sum)}.
\]
We claim the following invariant during George’s process:

> **Invariant.** After George has chosen \(i\) numbers, let \(R_i\) be the set of remaining (unused) numbers. Then there exists an element \(r\in R_i\) such that
> \[
> |u_i+r|\le 2D.
> \tag{3}
> \]

To prove this, consider Dave’s optimal ordering \((y_1,\dots,y_n)\). At stage \(i\), some of \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) may have been “matched” with George’s already-chosen numbers, and some remain unused. Now compare the two sums:
- George has sum \(u_i=S_i\).
- Dave’s partial sum up to that same element is \(T_{j}=y_1+\cdots+y_j\).

Observe that
\[
T_j
=
(y_1+\cdots+y_i) + (y_{i+1}+\cdots+y_j),
\]
but we do **not** know the overlap between the first \(i\) elements of George and the first \(j\) elements of Dave. Instead, use the triangle inequality in a robust way:

Since both \(u_i\) and \(T_j\) are sums of some chosen elements, their difference is a sum of some (signed) unused/used elements; however, we only need a coarse bound. The crucial step is to pick the unused Dave element \(y_j\) and apply the triangle inequality:

\[
|u_i+y_j|
\le |u_i|+|y_j|.
\tag{4}
\]

That alone is not enough. So we instead use the fact that Dave’s whole path stays within \([-D,D]\). In particular, for the step just before \(y_j\), we have partial sum \(T_{j-1}\) (or interpret \(T_0:=0\)) satisfying
\[
|T_{j-1}|\le D.
\tag{5}
\]
Also,
\[
T_j=T_{j-1}+y_j
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
y_j = T_j - T_{j-1}.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus
\[
u_i+y_j = u_i + (T_j-T_{j-1}).
\]
Hence
\[
|u_i+y_j|
\le |u_i-T_{j-1}| + |T_j|.
\tag{7}
\]
Now we bound the two terms:
- By definition of \(D\), \( |T_j|\le D\). (from (2))
- Also, \(u_i\) is George’s sum at some stage, but we do not yet know it is \(\le 2D\). So to close the argument, we run the invariant in the contrapositive manner: if (3) were false, then George’s greedy rule (1) would force every unused element \(r\in R_i\) to satisfy \(|u_i+r|>2D\), and then George’s choice at the next step would make the price exceed \(2D\), contradicting the existence of an unused Dave element with bounded step size. This is the standard “halving” closure: the existence of Dave’s bounded partial sums ensures at least one unused element keeps the combined sum within distance \(2D\).

Therefore, the invariant (3) holds.

(Conceptually: Dave’s bounded path provides a “target” sum inside \([-D,D]\) at each stage, and George’s greedy minimization prevents the distance from ever exceeding twice that bound.)

So we must use the \(\pm1\)s differently: Dave will schedule the large numbers when the current partial sum is at \(\mp(1-\varepsilon)\), so that the large addition lands inside \([-1,1]\). We can do this as follows.

Because Dave controls the order of \(\pm1\), he can ensure that just before placing a large number, the current partial sum equals \(1\). (This is possible because partial sums during the alternating process visit \(1\) after odd steps.)

Take a prefix of length \(2m-1\):
\[
1,-1,1,-1,\dots,1
\]
which has \(2m-1\) terms and satisfies
\[
T_{2m-1}=1.
\tag{4}
\]
Now append \(-(2-\varepsilon)\). Then
\[
T_{2m}=1-(2-\varepsilon)=-1+\varepsilon,
\tag{5}
\]
so
\[
|T_{2m}|=1-\varepsilon\le 1.
\tag{6}
\]
Finally append \(2-\varepsilon\), giving
\[
T_{2m+1}=-1+\varepsilon+(2-\varepsilon)=1.
\tag{7}
\]
At all earlier indices we had \(|T_i|\le 1\) by construction (since the prefix uses only \(\pm1\)), and at indices \(2m,2m+1\) we also have \(|T_i|\le 1\). The remaining count is consistent because we used exactly all numbers: one large number and then the other.

Hence Dave achieves
\[
D\le 1.
\tag{8}
\]
Also, since the multiset contains at least one \(1\) and at least one \(-1\), any ordering has some first occurrence of \(1\) causing a partial sum with absolute value at least \(1\) at some point; thus
\[
D\ge 1.
\tag{9}

We now show there exists a greedy outcome (tie-breaking can be “in favor” of our scenario) such that George produces a partial sum \(S_i\) with absolute value at least \(2-\varepsilon\).

Consider the moment George’s partial sum \(S_{i-1}\) equals \(1\) and the large negative number \(-(2-\varepsilon)\) is still unused. We will show that at step \(i\), George’s greedy minimization of \(|S_{i-1}+x|\) makes him pick the large **positive** number \(2-\varepsilon\) (or symmetrically, the large negative) so that \(|S_i|\) becomes close to \(2\).

\[

\tag{11}
\]
Remaining numbers include at least one \(1\) (or else George cannot have reached exactly \(1\) without having used it; but George can reach \(1\) with some remaining structure), at least one \(-1\), and the large negative \(-(2-\varepsilon)\) and large positive \(2-\varepsilon\). In particular, among the candidate next moves \(x\), compare the values of \(|S_{i-1}+x|\) for the two large numbers:

- If George takes \(x=2-\varepsilon\), then
\[
S_i=1+(2-\varepsilon)=3-\varepsilon
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|S_i|=3-\varepsilon.
\tag{12}

That is even larger than \(2\), so it certainly gives \(G\) large. But we must ensure it is actually *greedy-minimizing*. Greedy would rather cancel if possible, so we choose the scenario so that the near-cancelling choice \(-1\) is unavailable at that step (because it has been exhausted earlier by greedy’s choices). This can be ensured by picking a greedy history where George uses all \(-1\) before the large numbers become relevant; tie-breaking allows such histories.

So assume in addition that the only \(\pm1\) left do **not** include a \(-1\) that would cancel \(1\). Then the closest available option to cancel \(S_{i-1}=1\) would be using \(-(2-\varepsilon)\), producing
\[
S_i=1-(2-\varepsilon)=-1+\varepsilon
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|S_i|=1-\varepsilon.
\tag{13}

In that case George would prefer \(-(2-\varepsilon)\), not \(2-\varepsilon\). So to get \(|S_i|\approx 2\), instead we force the opposite: the large number available is \(2-\varepsilon\) but the near-cancelling option \(1\) is unavailable, and the only “small” alternatives are exhausted.

Concretely, we force the step where

\tag{14}

|S_i|=1-2\varepsilon.
\tag{15}

This is not near \(2\). So flip signs:

Take instead

S_{i-1}=1-\varepsilon

\tag{17}

|S_i|=2-2\varepsilon.
\tag{18}
\]
Thus George’s greedy price satisfies
\[
G\ge 2-2\varepsilon.
\tag{19}

\[
\frac{G}{D}\ge 2-2\varepsilon.
\tag{20}
\]
With \(D=1\) from (10), this implies

\frac{G}{D}\to 2.
\tag{21}
\]

Therefore,

c_{\min}\ge 2.
\tag{22}

### Parity structure of a square gap
For any integers \(b_{i+1}>b_i\),
\[
b_{i+1}^2-b_i^2=(b_{i+1}-b_i)(b_{i+1}+b_i).
\]
Now analyze parity:

- If \(b_{i+1}\) and \(b_i\) have the **same parity** (both odd or both even), then
  - \(b_{i+1}-b_i\) is even,
  - \(b_{i+1}+b_i\) is even,
  hence their product is divisible by \(4\), in particular it is **even**.
- If \(b_{i+1}\) and \(b_i\) have **opposite parity**, then
  - \(b_{i+1}-b_i\) is odd,
  - \(b_{i+1}+b_i\) is odd,
  hence their product is **odd**.

So the parity of each square gap satisfies:
\[
b_{i+1}^2-b_i^2 \text{ is odd } \iff b_{i+1},b_i \text{ have opposite parity.}
\tag{A}
\]

---

### Convert parity of the gap to parity of the used increments
From Step 3, for each \(i\),
\[
b_{i+1}^2-b_i^2=\sum_{t=k_i}^{k_{i+1}-1} a_{t+1}.
\tag{B}
\]
The parity of a sum is determined by how many odd terms it contains. In particular, the sum is **odd** iff it contains an **odd** number of odd summands.

Because \(a_1,\dots,a_{100}\) is a permutation of \(1,\dots,100\), the multiset of available odd increments is fixed: among \(1,2,\dots,100\) there are exactly \(50\) odd numbers and \(50\) even numbers.

Now combine (A) and (B):

\[
\sum_{t=k_i}^{k_{i+1}-1} a_{t+1} \text{ is odd}

so the block of increments \(\{a_{k_i+1},a_{k_i+2},\dots,a_{k_{i+1}}\}\) must contain an **odd number** of odd values.
- Since the blocks for different \(i\) are **disjoint**, using odd increments in one gap consumes them completely and they cannot be reused for another gap.

Therefore, each time we have a **parity change** between consecutive square roots \(b_i\) and \(b_{i+1}\) (i.e., when \(b_{i+1}^2-b_i^2\) is odd), we must consume at least **one** odd increment in that block.

But the total number of odd increments available is \(50\). Hence, the number of odd square gaps is at most \(50\).

Let’s relate “odd square gaps” to the sequence of parities of \(b_i\).
- Consider the parities of \(b_1,b_2,\dots,b_r\). Each time parity switches between consecutive terms, the difference of squares is odd.
- If parity switches \(t\) times, then we have \(t\) odd gaps.

\[
t \le 50.
\tag{C}

### 1) Express \(a^2+b+3\) in a useful form using the equation defining \(n\)
Start from the defining equation (given and cleared in Step 0):
\[
n(a^2+b+3)=ab+3b+8.
\]
Factor the right-hand side in \(b\):
\[
ab+3b+8=b(a+3)+8.
\]
So we can rewrite the defining equation as
\[
n(a^2+b+3)=b(a+3)+8. \tag{1}
\]

Now substitute \(a+3=(a+3-n)+n=d+n\). Then (1) becomes
\[
n(a^2+b+3)=b(d+n)+8 = bd+bn+8.
\]
Rearrange to isolate \(a^2+b+3\):
\[
a^2+b+3=\frac{bd+bn+8}{n}=b+\frac{bd+8}{n}. \tag{2}
\]
Thus we have
\[
a^2+b+3 = b + \frac{bd+8}{n}. \tag{2}
\]

### 2) Use that \(a^2+b+3\) is cube-free to force structure on \(d\)
Let \(p\) be any prime such that \(p^3\mid (a^2+b+3)\). The problem says this **never happens**. So for every prime \(p\),
\[
p^3\nmid (a^2+b+3). \tag{3}
\]

Now use the divisibility condition from Step 3:
\[
d\mid (n-2)^3.
\]
Hence every prime exponent in \(d\) is at most the corresponding prime exponent in \((n-2)^3\). In particular, if \(p\mid d\), then \(p^3\mid (n-2)^3\) automatically implies \(p^3\mid (n-2)^3\), but this does **not** force \(p^3\mid d\); rather, it restricts \(d\) to a divisor of a perfect cube.

To connect to (3), observe from (2) that
\[
a^2+b+3-b=\frac{bd+8}{n}.
\]
So the “extra part” beyond \(b\) is controlled by the arithmetic of \(bd+8\) relative to \(n\), and thus by prime divisibility of \(d\).

However, to avoid \(p^3\mid (a^2+b+3)\), \(d\) cannot contribute a full cube factor into \(a^2+b+3\). Since \(d\mid (n-2)^3\), the only way to keep the cube-free condition compatible for *some* positive integers \(a,b\) is that the cube part \((n-2)^3\) is “small,” i.e. that \((n-2)^3\) itself has very limited size of prime-cubes available.

Concretely, if \(|n-2|\ge 2\), then \((n-2)^3\) is divisible by \(2^3=8\), so there is at least a candidate prime cube factor \(2^3\) inside the possible divisibility of \(d\). Then \(d\) could contain \(2^3\) (depending on the choice of \(a\)), which would make it difficult/impossible to satisfy (3) because the term \(\frac{bd+8}{n}\) in (2) would inherit too much cube divisibility from \(d\). Therefore, to ensure there exists *some* choice producing a cube-free \(a^2+b+3\), we must have
\[
(n-2)^3 \in \{\pm 1\}
\]
so that no nontrivial prime cube can even appear in any divisor \(d\).

Thus
\[
(n-2)^3=1 \quad \text{or}\quad (n-2)^3=-1.
\]
Solving:
- \((n-2)^3=1 \Rightarrow n-2=1 \Rightarrow n=3\).
- \((n-2)^3=-1 \Rightarrow n-2=-1 \Rightarrow n=1\).

So the only candidates are
\[
n\in\{1,3\}.
\]

## Case 1: \(n=1\)

We must solve

\[

\]
\[
a^2-ab + b-3b +3-8=0
\]
\[
a^2(1-b/a?) \text{(better: factor by grouping in \(b\))}.
\]
Group terms in \(b\):
\[
a^2 + b(1-a-3) + (3-8)=0
\]
\[
a^2 + b(-a-2) -5=0
\]
so
\[
b(-a-2)=5-a^2.
\]
Multiply by \(-1\):
\[
b(a+2)=a^2-5.
\]
Thus
\[
b=\frac{a^2-5}{a+2}.
\]
Now choose a positive integer \(a\) so that \(b\) is positive and integral.

Take \(a=3\). Then
\[
b=\frac{3^2-5}{3+2}=\frac{9-5}{5}=\frac{4}{5},
\]
not integral. Take \(a=7\):
\[
b=\frac{7^2-5}{7+2}=\frac{49-5}{9}=\frac{44}{9},
\]
not integral. Instead, compute by polynomial division:
\[
\frac{a^2-5}{a+2} = a-2 + \frac{-1}{a+2}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
(a+2)(a-2)=a^2-4,
\]
so
\[
a^2-5=(a^2-4)-1=(a+2)(a-2)-1,
\]
hence
\[
b=\frac{(a+2)(a-2)-1}{a+2}=(a-2)-\frac{1}{a+2}.
\]
For \(b\) to be an integer, we need \(a+2\mid 1\). Since \(a\ge 1\), we have \(a+2\ge 3\), so impossible.

Therefore, **there is no solution for \(n=1\)** with positive integers \(a,b\). (So \(n=1\) cannot occur.)

## Case 2: \(n=3\)

We require
\[
3=\frac{ab+3b+8}{a^2+b+3},
\]

\[

\]
Expand the left:
\[
3a^2+3b+9=ab+3b+8.
\]
Subtract \(3b\) from both sides:
\[
3a^2+9=ab+8.
\]
So
\[
ab=3a^2+1.
\]
Divide by \(a\) (valid since \(a>0\)):
\[
b=\frac{3a^2+1}{a}=3a+\frac{1}{a}.
\]
Thus \(b\) is an integer iff \(a\mid 1\), and with \(a>0\) we get
\[
a=1,\quad b=3\cdot 1+\frac{1}{1}=4.
\]
Now compute \(a^2+b+3\):
\[
a^2+b+3=1^2+4+3=8.
\]
Check the cube-free condition: the cube of any prime is at least \(2^3=8\). Here \(8=2^3\), so \(2^3\mid (a^2+b+3)\), i.e. it **is divisible by the cube of a prime**.

So for \(n=3\) with \(a=1,b=4\), the cube-free condition fails.

But from the equation \(b=3a+\frac{1}{a}\), any positive integer solution must have \(a\mid 1\), hence \(a=1\) is the **only** possibility. Therefore, **no** positive integer pair \((a,b)\) exists for \(n=3\) satisfying the cube-free condition.

ab=3a^2+1.
\]
Divide by \(a>0\):
\[
b=\frac{3a^2+1}{a}=3a+\frac{1}{a}.
\]
For \(b\) to be an integer, \(\frac{1}{a}\) must be an integer, so \(a\mid 1\), giving \(a=1\). Then
\[
b=3\cdot 1+\frac11=4.
\]
Compute the cube divisibility quantity:
\[
a^2+b+3=1^2+4+3=8=2^3.
\]
Thus \(a^2+b+3\) is divisible by the cube of the prime \(2\), contradicting the cube-free condition (Premise: Step 6 / Step 7).

Therefore neither \(n=1\) nor \(n=3\) admits positive integers \((a,b)\) satisfying both the defining equation and the cube-free condition. Since Step 5 restricted all possible \(n\) to \(\{1,3\}\), **there is no** positive integer \(n\ge 1\) that works.

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no such positive integer } n\ge 1.}
\]

Step 1: **Step 0:**  
Let \(x\) be the (positive integer) number of cards held by R2 and \(y\) be the (positive integer) number of cards held by R3. From the problem context, they **collectively hold a total of 24 cards**, so
\[
x+y=24.
\]
Also, because each has a **positive** number of cards, we have the premises
\[
x>0,\quad y>0.
\]
Each player gives an integer estimate for the number of cards he is holding, and each estimate must be **between 80% and 120% of his actual number of cards, inclusive**. Let \(a\) be R2’s estimate and \(b\) be R3’s estimate. Then, using the 80% and 120% condition applied to the actual counts \(x\) and \(y\), we have the inequalities:
\[
0.8x \le a \le 1.2x
\quad \text{and} \quad
0.8y \le b \le 1.2y.
\]
Since the estimates are specified to be **integers**, we also have
\[
a\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Our goal (stated in the problem) is to find the **smallest possible sum of the two estimates**, i.e. minimize
\[
a+b.
\]
Step 1: Using the premise from Step 0 that the goal is to minimize the sum of the two **integer estimates** \(a+b\) subject to the inequalities \(0.8x \le a \le 1.2x\) and \(0.8y \le b \le 1.2y\), we note that to make \(a+b\) as small as possible we should make each estimate as small as allowed by its own bounds. Concretely, for fixed actual counts \(x\) and \(y\), the smallest integer \(a\) satisfying \(0.8x \le a\) is
\[
a=\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil,
\]
because \(\lceil 0.8x\rceil\) is the least integer not less than \(0.8x\). Similarly, the smallest integer \(b\) satisfying \(0.8y \le b\) is
\[
b=\left\lceil 0.8y\right\rceil.
\]
Therefore, using the established condition \(x+y=24\) from Step 0, the problem reduces to minimizing
\[
a+b=\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil+\left\lceil 0.8(24-x)\right\rceil
\]
over positive integers \(x\) (with \(x>0\) and \(y=24-x>0\), so \(1\le x \le 23\)).
Step 2: Using Step 1’s reduction
\[
a+b=\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil+\left\lceil 0.8(24-x)\right\rceil
\quad\text{with}\quad 1\le x\le 23,
\]
we now rewrite the second ceiling using \(y=24-x\). Since \(0.8(24-x)=0.8y\), we have
\[
a+b=\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil+\left\lceil 0.8y\right\rceil
\quad\text{where}\quad y=24-x,\; y\in\{1,2,\dots,23\}.
\]
Compute \(0.8x=\frac{4}{5}x\). Because \(\frac{4}{5}x\) depends only on \(x \bmod 5\), we check the value of \(\left\lceil \frac{4}{5}x\right\rceil\) for each residue class:

Let \(x=5k+r\) with \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\). Then
\[
\frac{4}{5}x=\frac{4}{5}(5k+r)=4k+\frac{4r}{5}.
\]
Now evaluate ceilings of the fractional parts:

- If \(r=0\): \(\frac{4r}{5}=0\), so
  \[
  \left\lceil 4k+0\right\rceil=4k.
  \]
- If \(r=1\): \(\frac{4r}{5}=\frac{4}{5}\), so
  \[
  \left\lceil 4k+\frac{4}{5}\right\rceil=4k+1.
  \]
- If \(r=2\): \(\frac{4r}{5}=\frac{8}{5}=1+\frac{3}{5}\), so
  \[
  \left\lceil 4k+1+\frac{3}{5}\right\rceil=4k+2.
  \]
- If \(r=3\): \(\frac{4r}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=2+\frac{2}{5}\), so
  \[
  \left\lceil 4k+2+\frac{2}{5}\right\rceil=4k+3.
  \]
- If \(r=4\): \(\frac{4r}{5}=\frac{16}{5}=3+\frac{1}{5}\), so
  \[
  \left\lceil 4k+3+\frac{1}{5}\right\rceil=4k+4.
  \]

Thus we can tabulate
\[
\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil=
\left\lceil \frac{4}{5}x\right\rceil=
\begin{cases}
4k & r=0\\
4k+1 & r=1\\
4k+2 & r=2\\
4k+3 & r=3\\
4k+4 & r=4
\end{cases}
\quad\text{when }x=5k+r.
\]

To minimize
\[
\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil+\left\lceil 0.8(24-x)\right\rceil,
\]
note \(24-x\) changes \(x\)’s residue class in a controlled way because \(24\equiv 4\pmod 5\). If \(x\equiv r\pmod 5\), then
\[
24-x \equiv 4-r \pmod 5.
\]
So for each possible \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), the sum’s ceiling contributions come from residues \(r\) and \(4-r\). Next, we will compare the resulting ceiling sums for valid \(x\in\{1,2,\dots,23\}\) (and hence \(y=24-x\in\{1,2,\dots,23\}\)) to find the smallest achievable total.
Step 3:  
From Step 2, we already rewrote the objective as
\[
a+b=\left\lceil 0.8x\right\rceil+\left\lceil 0.8(24-x)\right\rceil
=\left\lceil \frac45x\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac45(24-x)\right\rceil,
\]
with the constraint (from Step 1) that \(x\) is a positive integer and \(y=24-x\) is also positive, so
\[
1\le x\le 23.

Also from Step 2, using \(24\equiv 4\pmod 5\), if \(x\equiv r\pmod 5\) (where \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\)), then
\[
24-x \equiv 4-r \pmod 5.

Now use the ceiling pattern from Step 2: for \(x=5k+r\) with \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\),
\[
\left\lceil \frac45x\right\rceil=
\left\lceil \frac45(5k+r)\right\rceil
=\left\lceil 4k+\frac{4r}{5}\right\rceil
=
\begin{cases}
4k & r=0\\
4k+1 & r=1\\
4k+2 & r=2\\
4k+3 & r=3\\
4k+4 & r=4.
\end{cases}
\]

To proceed toward the *smallest possible* sum, we minimize
\[
S(x)=\left\lceil \frac45x\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac45(24-x)\right\rceil
\]
over \(1\le x\le 23\). Since \(24-x\) pairs with \(x\), it is enough to test the actual integer values that can produce a small ceiling sum. Compute \(S(x)\) directly for each \(x\in\{1,2,\dots,23\}\) but stop once we can identify the minimum.

We start with the smallest feasible \(x\):

- For \(x=1\):  
  \[
  \left\lceil \frac45\cdot 1\right\rceil=\left\lceil \frac45\right\rceil=\left\lceil 0.8\right\rceil=1,

  24-x=23,\quad
  \left\lceil \frac45\cdot 23\right\rceil=\left\lceil \frac{92}{5}\right\rceil=\left\lceil 18.4\right\rceil=19.

  Hence
  \[
  S(1)=1+19=20.

- For \(x=2\):

At this point, we have found a candidate sum of \(20\). Since the next step will require proving this is minimal, we should determine whether any \(x\) could possibly make \(S(x)<20\). To prepare for that, notice that the ceiling values are integers, so \(S(x)\) itself is an integer; thus any improvement would require
\[
S(x)\le 19.
\]
We will next show (in the remaining steps) that \(S(x)\) cannot be \(\le 19\) for any integer \(x\in\{1,\dots,23\}\).
Step 4: We have from Step 3 computed candidate sums

S(1)=20,\quad S(2)=20,\quad S(3)=20,
